title: Pandas Data Loading: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on loading data into pandas from CSV, Excel, JSON, Parquet and SQL. Covers key read options, dtype control on load, chunked reading of large files, common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Loading Data: The Mental Model
points: Every reader is pd.read_* and returns a DataFrame; every writer is df.to_* with a matching format
Pipeline: source (file, URL, buffer, DB) → parser → type inference → DataFrame with RangeIndex
Text formats (CSV, JSON) store no types so pandas infers them; Parquet and SQL carry a schema so types survive
Memory cost is set at load time: dtype, usecols and chunksize decide whether a file fits in RAM
Choose the format by need: CSV for interchange, Parquet for analytics, JSON for APIs, SQL for live tables, Excel for business users

chapters.title: read_csv Options That Matter
points: sep, header, names, index_col: sep=';' for semicolon files, header=None plus names=[...] when the file has no header row
usecols=['a','b'] loads only those columns, saving memory and parse time
nrows=1000 and skiprows=n peek at a huge file or skip junk lines before the header
na_values=['NA','-'] and keep_default_na control which strings become NaN; true_values/false_values map to bool
parse_dates=['col'] with date_format='%Y-%m-%d' parses dates at load; otherwise they stay as object strings
encoding='utf-8' or 'latin-1' fixes UnicodeDecodeError; compression is inferred from .gz/.zip extension

chapters.title: dtypes on Load and chunksize
points: dtype={'id':'int32','city':'category'} sets types at parse time and avoids slow inference passes
Low-cardinality strings as category cut memory massively; downcast ints/floats to int8/int32/float32 when range allows
Nullable dtypes 'Int64', 'string', 'boolean' keep missing values without turning ints into float64; dtype_backend='pyarrow' uses Arrow-backed types
Mixed-type column warning (DtypeWarning) means inference ran per chunk: pass dtype explicitly or low_memory=False
chunksize=100_000 returns an iterator of DataFrames: for chunk in pd.read_csv(f, chunksize=n): aggregate each, then combine partial results
Process chunks by filtering or aggregating, never by appending all chunks to a list, or memory use is the same as a full load

chapters.title: Excel, JSON and Parquet
points: pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name='Sales', usecols='A:D', header=1) needs openpyxl for .xlsx; sheet_name=None returns a dict of all sheets
JSON orient controls shape: 'records' = list of row dicts, 'columns' = {col:{idx:val}}, 'index', 'split' = {index, columns, data}, 'table' includes schema
pd.read_json(path, orient='records', lines=True) reads newline-delimited JSON; pd.json_normalize(data) flattens nested dicts into columns
to_parquet/read_parquet(engine='pyarrow') stores a typed columnar format, compressed (snappy default), preserving dtypes and datetimes
read_parquet(path, columns=['a','b']) reads only chosen columns and filters= pushes row filters down, so it beats CSV on speed and size
Parquet needs pyarrow or fastparquet installed; partition_cols writes a directory split by column values

chapters.title: read_sql with SQLAlchemy
points: engine = create_engine('postgresql+psycopg2://user:pw@host/db') builds the connection; pandas needs SQLAlchemy for non-sqlite databases
pd.read_sql(text('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id > :min'), engine, params={'min': 10}) runs a query into a DataFrame
Always use params for values; never f-string user input into SQL because of injection risk
read_sql_query takes a SQL string and read_sql_table takes a table name; read_sql dispatches to either
index_col, parse_dates and dtype work like read_csv; chunksize returns an iterator of DataFrames for large result sets
df.to_sql('t', engine, if_exists='append', index=False, method='multi') writes back; the default if_exists='fail' raises if the table exists

chapters.title: Loading Data Cheat Sheet
points: CSV: read_csv(f, sep, usecols, dtype, parse_dates, na_values, nrows, chunksize, encoding)
Excel: read_excel(f, sheet_name, usecols, header) needs openpyxl; sheet_name=None gives dict of DataFrames
JSON: read_json(f, orient, lines=True) and json_normalize for nested data
Parquet: read_parquet(f, columns, filters) with pyarrow; keeps dtypes, smallest and fastest
SQL: read_sql(text(q), engine, params, chunksize); to_sql(name, engine, if_exists, index=False)
Big files: usecols + dtype (category, int32) + chunksize with per-chunk aggregation; prefer Parquet over CSV for repeat loads
